content.chapter: Chapter 1: What Was the Ahî Organization?
objectives: Say what the Ahî Organization was and when it started.
Name three jobs of the group in trade.
Use past verbs with -ed (started, organized, checked).
content.pedagogy: The chapter introduces a new idea: a group of workers and masters that organized work life. A short chart (when and where / what it did) gives learners the key facts before the next chapter adds character.
priorKnowledge: The words shop, work and price.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The Ahî Organization was not a school building; it was a group of workers and masters.
“Apprentice” means a young learner, not a master.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: past -ed verbs (started, played, guided, organized, checked, solved)
Look (Activity 1): It checked the quality of goods.
Practise (Activity 2): fill started, organized and checked.
Likely errors: *it check yesterday · *startted.
Use (Activity 3): a group in my school.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: a-HÎ, a-na-TO-li-a.
Stress: ap-PREN-ti-ces, OR-ga-nized.
Endings: checked /tʃekt/, solved /sɒlvd/, started /ˈstɑːrtɪd/.
beforeReading: Ask: “Who teaches a young person a job? Where?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the Ahî Organization?
Second reading: complete the chart: when and where / what it did.
Find three things the group did as a trade group.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a group in my school; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: When and where did the group start?
Who worked in the workshops?
What did the group do as a trade group?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Anatolia” and “Workshops” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: trade, guided, apprentices, goods, set prices, solved.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one example in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write three sentences about a market in your town today: who sells, who buys and who checks the prices.

expectedResponses: The Ahî Organization was a religious, social and trade group. It started in Anatolia in the 13th century. It checked goods, set prices and solved business problems.
content.transferTask: Talk about a group or club in your school.
content.teacherReflection: Can learners say what the group was and name its jobs in trade?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with a past -ed verb about the Ahî Organization.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
columns: What did it do at work?
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about the Ahî Organization. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads the first three sentences and B reads the last three. Each tells the partner two facts without looking. The partner writes them down, then both check in the text.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads the last sentence. Asker asks “What did the group do as a trade group?” Checker checks the three answers in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor asks, “What was the Ahî Organization?” The learner answers in three short sentences: what it was, when and where it started, and one thing it did.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “In workshops, this group organized work life for apprentices, experienced workers, and masters.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Ahî Organization was and when and where it started. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter says the group was religious, social, and trade. Which sentences tell us about trade?” (Quality of goods, prices and business problems are about trade.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name when and where the group started and two of its jobs at work.

thinkAloud.strategy: Find the meaning of a word
thinkAloud.sentence: In workshops, this group organized work life for apprentices, experienced workers, and masters.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I see “apprentices” in a list with “experienced workers” and “masters”. Masters know a lot. So apprentices are probably the people at the start, the young learners. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “It started in Anatolia in the 13th century and played a big role in the founding of the Ottoman Empire.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: When and where did the group start?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Which group or club in your school helps students?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her group.

objectives: Name good behaviors that members had.
Name two things members did not do.
Say how members learned good manners.
Use had to and did not for rules in the past.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows the second side of the group: good character. Learners list what members did and did not do, then connect the rules with their own class rules.
priorKnowledge: Past simple; did not + base verb.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Members did not only work; they also learned good manners for daily life.
“Role models” are people you learn from by watching them, not teachers in a classroom.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: had to · did not · past -ed verbs (encouraged, helped, learned)
Look (Activity 1): Members had to be honest.
Practise (Activity 2): fill the rules.
Likely errors: *had to honest · *did not drank.
Use (Activity 3): rules in my class.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: GEN-er-ous, THANK-ful, en-COUR-aged, for-BID-den.
Linking: “had to” /ˈhæd tə/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What makes a good person? Say two words.”
duringReading: First reading: Why was character important in the group?
Second reading: make two lists: members did / members did not.
Find two examples of good manners.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Two lists; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: rules in my class; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why was character important in the group?
What did members stay away from?
What good manners did members learn?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Honest Members” and “Visiting the Sick” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: encouraged, forbidden, tell lies, good manners.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the two lists with one example in each.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write three rules for a good shop today.

formativeAssessment: Names one thing members did not do.
expectedResponses: Members had to be honest, generous and thankful. They helped people in need. They did not drink alcohol or tell lies.
content.transferTask: Talk about the rules in your class.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the rules of the group with rules in their own lives?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “had to” about the Ahî members.

rubricLevels.secure: Says what members did not do.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say three sentences about good Ahî members. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads the first two sentences and B reads the last three. Each tells the partner one rule of the group without looking. The partner says if it is something members did or did not do.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads the sentence about members’ character. Asker asks “What did members have to be?” Checker checks the three words in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A new student asks, “What are the rules in your class?” The learner compares them with the rules of the Ahî members in two sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “Members had to be honest, generous, and thankful.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, three good things Ahî members did and one thing they did not do. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer say ‘For example’ in the middle of the chapter?” (To show which actions were forbidden.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners name two good habits of members and one thing they stayed away from.

thinkAloud.sentence: For example, they did not drink alcohol or tell lies.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “For example” tells me that the next words are examples. The sentence before it says members stayed away from forbidden actions. So alcohol and lies are two forbidden actions. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “With the help of role models, members learned good manners for daily life, such as walking on the street or visiting sick people.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: How did members learn good manners?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What good manners do people need in your town today?
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate which of his or her manners you also think are important.

objectives: Explain the steps from apprentice to master.
Say why training was very important in Ahî culture.
Compare Ahî organizations with madrasas and dervish schools.
Use until, so and not just … but.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows that learning a job also meant learning to be a good person. The idea of shame for a job done badly can start a discussion about responsibility at work.
anticipatedMisconceptions: People did not start a business before they were ready; they did not skip levels.
Ahî organizations were like schools, but they were not madrasas.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: until · so · but · not just … (but also)
Look (Activity 1): until they became masters.
Practise (Activity 2): choose so, but or until.
Likely errors: *until they become (past) · *so because.
Use (Activity 3): a skill I am learning.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: ap-PREN-ti-ces, CUL-tur-al, MAD-ra-sas.
Linking: “started as” /ˈstɑːrtɪdæz/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What skill would you like to learn from a master?”
duringReading: First reading: How did young people learn a job?
Second reading: draw three steps: apprentice → levels → master.
Find why training was important.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Three steps; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: a skill I am learning; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did people not start a business before they were ready?
What else did members learn, not just a job?
How were Ahî organizations like schools?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Masters” and “Schools for the People” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: masters, grow, effect, personal, cultural, organizations, training, experts, shame, wise.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three steps with the first one filled in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write four sentences about how you learn a skill, with until and so.

expectedResponses: Young people started as apprentices and went through levels until they became masters. Training was very important, so they did not start a business before they were ready.
content.transferTask: Write about a skill you are learning.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners link learning a job with being a good person?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “until” and one with “so”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell a partner how a young person became a master. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: One learner reads paragraph 1 and explains to a partner why people did not start a business early. The partner says it in one sentence with “because”.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads paragraph 2. Listener notes what people learned in Ahî organizations. Writer writes the two things on the board.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A classmate asks, “Where do young people learn a job in your town today?” The learner answers and compares it with the Ahî organizations.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “They were important cultural centers where people learned a job and how to be a good person.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, how a young person in an Ahî organization became a master. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why does the writer compare Ahî organizations with madrasas and dervish schools?” (They were also places where people learned.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: The steps are in the right order: apprentice, different levels, master. Learners use “so” once.

thinkAloud.sentence: So, training to learn a job was very important, and people did not start a business before they were ready.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The sentence starts with “So”. That means the reason is in the sentence before. Not learning a job correctly brought shame. So people trained for a long time first. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “But their training was not just about learning a job.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What else did young people learn?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Who taught you an important skill?
onlineTask.reply: Ask your classmate one question about his or her teacher.

objectives: Say what the Ahî Organization wanted from every shop owner.
Explain why the shoes broke and why the customers were angry.
Use so, after + time and to + verb (reason).
content.pedagogy: The first half of a short, memorable story. Learners meet the problem: a shoemaker chooses money over quality. Stop at the end of the chapter and let learners guess what the Ahî leader will do.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of irregular verbs (broke, went, saw).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The customers did not go to the shoemaker; they went to the Ahî leader.
The leather was cheap, not the price of the shoes.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: so · after + time · to + verb (reason)
Look (Activity 1): so he began using cheap leather.
Practise (Activity 2): tell the story with so, after and to.
Likely errors: *for complain · *after few weeks.
Use (Activity 3): honest work.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: SHOE-mak-er, CUS-tom-ers, com-PLAIN.
Past forms: broke /broʊk/, saw /sɔː/.
beforeReading: Ask: “What do you do when something you bought breaks very fast?”
duringReading: First reading: What was the problem?
Second reading: put three events in order.
Find what the Ahî Organization wanted from shop owners.
afterReading: Ask: “What will the Ahî leader do?” Learners write one guess for Chapter 5.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Story order; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: honest work; 38–40 Guess for Chapter 5.
discussionPoints: What did the Ahî Organization want from every shop owner?
Why did the shoemaker use cheap leather?
Why were the customers angry?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Shoemaker” and “Angry Customers” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: quality work, customers, broke, to complain, honest, owner, leader.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the three events on cards to order.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write what the customers said to the Ahî leader in two sentences.

formativeAssessment: Uses so or to + verb correctly.
expectedResponses: A shoemaker used cheap leather, so his shoes broke after a few weeks. The customers became angry and went to the Ahî leader to complain.
content.transferTask: Write about honest work in a shop today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see the link between cheap leather and angry customers?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “so” about the shoemaker.

rubricLevels.secure: Explains why the customers were angry.
rubricLevels.notYet: Point to “broke after only a few weeks”.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell the shoemaker’s problem in three steps. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each retells the part with books closed. The partner asks one “Why?” question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “Why were the customers angry?” Checker finds the answer in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A customer in a shop today buys shoes that break. The learner tells the shop owner what is wrong, politely, in two sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “They wanted every shop owner to do honest and quality work.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the shoemaker did and why his customers were angry. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter begins with what the group wanted. Why does the writer tell us this before the story?” (So we can see that the shoemaker did the opposite.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners use “so” once in their retelling. They give the right order of events.

thinkAloud.sentence: In a small town, a shoemaker wanted to make more money, so he began using cheap leather.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I see “so”. The part after “so” is the result. He wanted more money, and the result was cheap leather. I can guess the shoes will not be good. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Soon, his customers saw a problem.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What problem did the customers see?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What do you do when you buy something that breaks?
onlineTask.reply: Give your classmate one more idea.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Shoe on the Roof
objectives: Say what the Ahî leader did with the shoes.
Explain why the shoes on the roof were a warning.
Explain where the saying ‘pabucu dama atılmak’ comes from.
Use if for a condition and its result.
content.pedagogy: The second half of the shoe story gives the leader’s answer and the moral: honest, quality work. It also explains a Turkish saying, so learners connect language and culture. The Turkish saying stays in quotation marks, as in the book.
priorKnowledge: Past simple of irregular verbs (threw, could).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The leader did not throw the shoemaker onto the roof; he threw the shoes.
The warning was for every shop owner, not only for this shoemaker.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: if + past, could not · past forms (walked, decided, threw)
Look (Activity 1): If he did not improve …
Practise (Activity 2): choose walked, decided and threw.
Likely errors: *throwed · *if he not improve.
Use (Activity 3): if you break a rule.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: im-PROVE, WARN-ing, LEAD-er.
Past form: threw /θruː/.
beforeReading: Ask: “In Chapter 4, the customers went to the Ahî leader. What do you think he did?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the leader do?
Second reading: find why it was a warning.
Find the Turkish saying.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Check the guesses from Chapter 4; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Why a warning?; 17–21 Quick Challenge; 21–32 Language Focus 1–2; 32–38 Use: if you break a rule; 38–40 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the leader throw the shoes onto the roof and not into the street?
What did the warning show?
What does the saying mean today?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Ahî Leader” and “On the Roof” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: poor-quality, low-quality, improve.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the sentence “If he did not improve …” with the two parts in two colors.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Retell Chapters 4 and 5 together in five sentences.

expectedResponses: The leader threw the low-quality shoes onto the roof. It was a warning for every shop owner. If the shoemaker did not improve, he could not sell shoes in that town again.
content.transferTask: Write about rules in your school with if.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners understand the link between the story and the saying?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “if” about the shoemaker.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners say what the Ahî leader did and why. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads up to “He decided to do something about it.” B reads the rest. Each retells the part with books closed. The partner asks one “Why?” question.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Reader reads the sentences about the leader. Asker asks “Where did he throw the shoes?” Checker finds the answer in the text.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A tourist hears the Turkish saying and asks what it means. The learner tells the story in three short sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “This was a big warning for every shop owner in town.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the Ahî leader did with the shoes and what the Turkish saying means. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “Why did the leader throw the shoes onto the roof and not into the street?” (Everyone in town could see them. It was a warning.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners explain the warning and use “if” once.

thinkAloud.sentence: If he did not improve the quality, he could not sell shoes in that town again.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: I see “If”. The first part is a condition, and the second part is the result. So the shoemaker had one choice: make better shoes. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “He threw the low-quality shoes onto the roof of the shop.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Where did the leader throw the shoes?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: Do you know another saying with a story behind it?
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate if he or she knew this saying.

objectives: Say what the apprentice wanted and what his master said.
Explain what went wrong in the new shop.
Say how the master answered when the apprentice came back.
Use not … yet, had to and did not.
content.pedagogy: The first half of a story about patience and humility. The apprentice does not listen, fails and comes back. Stop at the end of the chapter: the secret is still hidden, and learners can guess it.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The apprentice did not get the certificate; he left without it.
The master forgave him; he did not send him away.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not … yet · had to · did not + base verb
Look (Activity 1): You are not ready yet.
Practise (Activity 2): choose listen, had and yet.
Likely errors: *I am not ready already · *did not listened · *had return.
Use (Activity 3): not ready yet.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: cer-TIF-i-cate, ap-PREN-tice, for-GAVE.
Intonation: “You are not ready yet.” — falling at the end.
beforeReading: Ask: “Did you ever start something before you were ready? What happened?”
duringReading: First reading: Why did the master say, “You are not ready yet”?
Second reading: make a chart: the request / the new shop / the return.
Find what happened to the glass.
afterReading: Ask: “Why did the glass crack?” Learners write one guess for Chapter 7.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Chart; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–33 Language Focus 1–2; 33–38 Use: not ready yet; 38–40 Guess for Chapter 7.
discussionPoints: What did the apprentice need before he opened his own shop?
Why did no one want to buy his work?
What did the master do when the apprentice came back?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Glassmaker” and “Cracked Glass” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: certificate, ready, cracked, forgave.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with one sentence in each column.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write what the apprentice thought on the way back to his master, in three sentences.

formativeAssessment: Uses not … yet or did not correctly.
expectedResponses: The apprentice wanted a certificate, but his master said, “You are not ready yet.” He did not listen and opened a shop in another city. His glass cracked, and he had to return to his master.
content.transferTask: Talk about something you are not ready for yet.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see why the master said “not yet” and not “never”?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “not … yet” about the apprentice.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses not … yet or did not.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners tell why the apprentice came back to his master. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraph 1 and B reads paragraph 2. Each tells the partner the part in two sentences. Together they put the events in order.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “What happened to the glass?” Checker reads the sentence with “cracked”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A younger student wants to stop a course early. The learner tells him or her the story of the apprentice in three sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “But his master shook his head and said, “You are not ready yet.”” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, what the young glassmaker did and why he came back to his master. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The chapter ends with ‘his kind master forgave him.’ Why does the writer use the word ‘kind’?” (It shows the master was not angry.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners say what went wrong in the new shop. They use “not … yet” once.

thinkAloud.sentence: All of his new glass cups and figures cracked after a short time.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: The sentence before says “But things went wrong.” This sentence tells me what went wrong. The next sentence gives the result: no one wanted to buy his work. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “But things went wrong.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: What went wrong in the new shop?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What can you not do yet, but want to learn?
onlineTask.reply: Give your classmate one idea to help him or her learn it.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: The Secret of the Glass
objectives: Retell what happened in the dark room in order.
Explain why the apprentice’s glass cracked.
Explain where the saying ‘püf noktası’ comes from.
Use because and to + verb (purpose).
content.pedagogy: The second half of the glass story gives the answer to the mystery from Chapter 6 and the value of a master’s knowledge. The apprentice’s return shows that learning takes time. The Turkish saying stays in quotation marks, as in the book.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The apprentice did not learn the secret before he left; he learned it after he returned.
The bubble disappeared because the master blew on it, not because of the sunlight.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: because · to + verb (purpose) · there was · past perfect for an earlier event (had made, had cracked) — recognize only
Look (Activity 1): because he had not blown out those tiny air bubbles.
Practise (Activity 2): choose to, was and because.
Likely errors: *for cool down · *there were a bubble.
Use (Activity 3): the secret of a skill.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Stress: dis-ap-PEARED, BUB-ble, CEIL-ing.
Sound: “Püf!” — say it softly, like the master.
beforeReading: Ask: “In Chapter 6, the glass cracked. Why do you think it cracked?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the master show the apprentice?
Second reading: put four events in the dark room in order.
Find the secret of the glass.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Check the guesses from Chapter 6; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Events in the dark room; 18–22 Quick Challenge; 22–33 Language Focus 1–2; 33–38 Use: the secret of a skill; 38–40 Exit ticket. (Theater in a second lesson.)
discussionPoints: Why did masters use a dark room?
What was inside the hot glass?
What did the apprentice understand at the end?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “The Dark Room” and “The Air Bubble” when the picture is in place.
The group task “Our Ahî Story Theater” closes the book.
Word Notes: cool down, ceiling, held up, tiny, bubble, inside, blew on, disappeared, key point of a job.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four events on cards to order.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write the story of Chapters 6 and 7 from the master’s point of view in five sentences.

expectedResponses: The master took the apprentice into a dark room and showed him a tiny air bubble in the glass. He blew on it, and the bubble disappeared. The apprentice’s glass had cracked because he had not blown out the bubbles.
content.transferTask: Talk about the secret of a skill you know.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners connect the story with patience and learning?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “because” about the glass.

noteTaking.focus: Second listening, books closed. Learners write one or two words in each box, not full sentences.
noteTaking.afterNotes: From the notes only, learners explain why the glass cracked and how the apprentice learned the secret. The partner checks one fact in the book.

mediationTasks.relay: Pairs: A reads paragraphs 1 and 2, B reads paragraph 3. Each tells the partner the part in three sentences. Together they explain the secret.
mediationTasks.pairRoles: Groups of three. Reader reads paragraph 2. Asker asks “What was inside the glass?” Checker reads the sentence with “Püf!”.
mediationTasks.cultureGuide: Role-play: A visitor at a glass shop asks, “What does ‘püf noktası’ mean?” The learner tells the story of the glass in three sentences.
mediationTasks.translation: Pairs put “At that moment, the apprentice understood his mistake.” into their home language. Which words were hard to put into the home language, and why?
mediationTasks.homeRetell: Homework: Learners tell someone at home, in their home language, the secret of the glass and what “püf noktası” means. Next lesson ask two learners what their listener asked.
mediationTasks.analysis: Ask: “The master says ‘You are not ready yet’ in Chapter 6 and ‘Now you are ready’ here. Why does the writer use these two sentences?” (They show that the apprentice learned and the master was right.)
mediationTasks.lookFor: Learners link the cracked glass with the air bubbles. They use “because” once.

thinkAloud.sentence: The glass pieces he had made before had cracked because he had not blown out those tiny air bubbles.
thinkAloud.model: Read it aloud, then think aloud: “Because” gives me the cause. The effect is the cracked glass. The cause is the air bubbles. Now I understand the title of the chapter. Learners try the same strategy with another sentence of the chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Learners stop after “Masters used this room to cool down hot glass slowly so it did not crack.”
stopAndCheck.question: Ask: Why did masters use the dark room?

onlineTask.post: Write two sentences: What is the “secret” of a job or a skill you know?
onlineTask.reply: Tell your classmate if you knew this secret.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization A2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: The Role of the Ahî Organization (Ahilik)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 7 chapter units of 40 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Young learners and adults who can read short, simple texts about people, work and values, and who can write short connected sentences.
metadata.purpose: Develop A2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the Ahî Organization: work, training and character in Anatolia, and two famous stories behind Turkish sayings, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned in small steps: in the Language Focus, learners first LOOK at a form in a real chapter sentence, then PRACTISE it in controlled, meaningful tasks, and finally USE it in short YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 7 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Look → Practise → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a picture or a word from daily life.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: description, steps or a story in order.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (look → practise → use), then a short production about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Text-based and in small steps. Start from the story sentence, ask a simple meaning question (What does this word show?), let learners answer, then confirm the rule and practice it in context. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: past -ed verbs (started, played, guided, organized, checked, solved)
Ch2: had to · did not · past -ed verbs (encouraged, helped, learned)
Ch3: until · so · but · not just … (but also)
Ch4: so · after + time · to + verb (reason)
Ch5: if + past, could not · past forms (walked, decided, threw)
Ch6: not … yet · had to · did not + base verb
Ch7: because · to + verb (purpose) · there was · past perfect for an earlier event (had made, had cracked) — recognize only

skillsFocus.listening: TYMM YDAB1: follow narration for gist, people and key events.
skillsFocus.reading: TYMM YDAB2: find key information, put events in order and understand simple reasons.
skillsFocus.speaking: TYMM YDAB3: describe rules, skills and people in short connected sentences.
skillsFocus.writing: TYMM YDAB4: write short connected sentences with and, but, so and because.

valuesFocus: D6 Honesty — Honest work and honest words.
D3 Diligence — Learning a job well before starting it.
D20 Helpfulness — Helping people in need.
D14 Respect — Respect for masters and teachers.
languageFocus: Every one of the 7 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Look → Practise → Use (3 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the thinking target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, picture cards, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for one more sentence or one more reason from the book, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
The Turkish sayings ‘pabucu dama atılmak’ and ‘püf noktası’ belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are.
Bracketed Turkish words in the text (çırak, medrese) belong to the teacher-approved story; they are read as they are.

globalCitizenship.title: Global Citizenship and Cultural Bridges
globalCitizenship.description: The Ahî Organization links medieval Anatolia with questions every community faces today: how to do honest work, how to train young workers and how to help people in need.

themes.title: Honest work:
themes.description: The shoemaker’s cheap shoes became a warning for every shop (Chapters 4 and 5). Discuss how customers are protected today.

themes.title: Learning from a master:
themes.description: Apprentices learned a job step by step (Chapters 3, 6 and 7). Compare this with training for jobs today.

themes.title: Helping others:
themes.description: Members helped people in need and visited sick people (Chapter 2). Discuss how people help each other in your town.

actions: Find one shop or workshop in your area and write two sentences about what it makes.
Make a short poster: “Five rules for a good worker”.
Ask an older family member how they learned their job.

exitTicket: One thing I learned about the Ahî Organization today is …
One new word from today’s chapter is …
One good action I can do this week is …

miniProject.title: Our Ahî Story Theater
miniProject.desc: In groups, choose one story: The Shoe on the Roof (Chapters 4–5) or The Secret of the Glass (Chapters 6–7). Write four short scenes, use one sentence from the book and explain the Turkish saying at the end.

reflectivePrompt.title: A Good Worker
reflectivePrompt.desc: The Ahî members were honest, generous and thankful (Chapter 2). Write four to five sentences about a good worker you know. What does this person do well?

valuesEducation.title: TYMM Values in Action
valuesEducation.description: Use only values the chapter really shows. Ask for the sentence first, then connect the value to a small action learners can do and see. See https://tymm.meb.gov.tr/beceriler/erdem-deger-eylem-cercevesi.

items.label: D6 Honesty
items.value: Honesty: Members did not tell lies, and the shoemaker’s cheap shoes were a warning for every shop (Chapters 2 and 5).

items.label: D3 Diligence
items.value: Diligence: Young people went through levels until they became masters (Chapters 3, 6 and 7).

items.label: D20 Helpfulness
items.value: Helpfulness: Members helped people in need and visited sick people (Chapter 2).

items.label: D14 Respect
items.value: Respect: The apprentice returned, said sorry and learned from his master (Chapters 6 and 7).

questions: What small action can show it this week?
Which part is from the book and which part is my own idea?

cefrProfile.intro: This book is written for CEFR A2. The table links the A2 descriptors of the End-of-Level Test A2 to the chapters of this book where learners practice them.

rows.descriptor: Can understand short, simple texts containing the highest frequency vocabulary, including a proportion of shared international vocabulary items.
practice: Chapter 3 (Training and Culture): Put the steps from apprentice to master in order.
Whole book: Knowledge Check and Final Challenge.

rows.descriptor: Can write a series of simple phrases and sentences linked with simple connectors like “and”, “but” and “because”.
practice: Chapter 4 (Bad Shoes): Write three sentences about honest work in a shop today.
Language Review, “Use: A Good Worker Today”: Write four to five sentences.

rows.descriptor: Can give a simple description or presentation of people, living or working conditions, daily routines, likes/dislikes, etc. as a short series of simple phrases and sentences linked into a list.
practice: Chapter 2 (Good Character): Tell your partner three rules in your class.
Chapter 7 (The Secret of the Glass): Act out a story in the class theater.

test.title: End-of-Level Test A2
test.when: Give the test when the class has finished the A2 books it reads this term. It has four parts and takes about 60 minutes plus a short speaking test for each learner.
parts: Reading and Language (40 minutes): in the app. The learner gets a test code at the end.
Writing (20 minutes): on paper. Write an email to a friend about a visit to an old place. (50–70 words)
Speaking (about 6 minutes): one learner with the teacher, in 2 parts.
Scoring: type the test code in “Score a test”, then score Writing and Speaking with the bands. Copy the pilot line for the pilot results sheet.

Find two things members did not do.
Find two examples of good manners.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “With the help of role models, members learned good manners for daily life, such as walking on the street or visiting sick people.”
stopAndCheck.question: How did members learn good manners? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

objectives: I can explain how young people learned a job.

discussionPoints: People did not start a business before they were ready. Why is it good to be ready before you start something?
interactiveTips: Open the picture hotspots “Masters” and “Schools for the People” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Read the second sentence again. Find started, went through and became. Order them again.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Language Focus, last activity: Write three sentences about a skill you are learning.

whatToNotice: Members also learned how to be good people.
readListen: What skill would you like to learn? Write one.
Read the chapter and find the steps.
Draw three steps: apprentice, levels, master.
findAnswerInStory: Find how young people started.
Find what not learning a job correctly brought.
Find what Ahî organizations worked as.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: masters, grow, effect, personal, cultural, organizations, training, experts, shame, wise.
“Until they became masters.” What is a master?
Write one sentence with grow.

wrongAnswerSupport: Find started, went through and became.
selfCheck: Can I explain the steps?

thinkAloud.sentence: So, training to learn a job was very important, and people did not start a business before they were ready.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “But their training was not just about learning a job.”
stopAndCheck.question: What else did young people learn? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

Put three events in order.

Find when the shoes broke.
Find where the customers went.

“They went to the Ahî leader to complain.” What does complain mean?
Write one sentence with customers.

selfCheck: Can I explain the problem?
Can I tell the events in order?
Can I use so and to + verb?

thinkAloud.sentence: In a small town, a shoemaker wanted to make more money, so he began using cheap leather.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: I see “so”. The part after “so” is the result. He wanted more money, and the result was cheap leather. I can guess the shoes will not be good. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Soon, his customers saw a problem.”
stopAndCheck.question: What problem did the customers see? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

content.chapter: Chapter 5: The Shoe on the Roof

content.lessonPlan: What do you think the leader did? Write one guess. Read the chapter and check your guess. Find why it was a warning.

The story explains a Turkish saying.

Find why it was a warning.
findAnswerInStory: Find what the leader looked at.
Find where he threw the shoes.
Find what the shoemaker had to do.
vocabularyInContext: Word Notes: poor-quality, low-quality, improve.
“Poor-quality” and “low-quality.” What do they mean?

selfCheck: Can I say what the leader did?
Can I explain the saying?
Can I use if?

thinkAloud.sentence: If he did not improve the quality, he could not sell shoes in that town again.

thinkAloud.sentence: The glass pieces he had made before had cracked because he had not blown out those tiny air bubbles.
thinkAloud.model: A good reader thinks: “Because” gives me the cause. The effect is the cracked glass. The cause is the air bubbles. Now I understand the title of the chapter. Try the same with another sentence of this chapter.

stopAndCheck.after: Stop after “Masters used this room to cool down hot glass slowly so it did not crack.”
stopAndCheck.question: Why did masters use the dark room? If you cannot say it, read that part again.

metadata.title: The Ahî Organization A2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 20 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: A2 learners who read about the Ahî Organization alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Understand the 7 chapters of The Ahî Organization.
Find evidence in the text before answering.
Understand what the Ahî Organization was and how young people learned a job.
Retell two stories and explain the Turkish sayings they come from.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 7.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One thing about the Ahî Organization that I liked:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 7 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 20 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 3 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows honesty, hard work, helpfulness and respect. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Honesty: Honesty: Members did not tell lies, and the shoemaker’s cheap shoes were a warning for every shop (Chapters 2 and 5).
Diligence: Diligence: Young people went through levels until they became masters (Chapters 3, 6 and 7).
Helpfulness: Helpfulness: Members helped people in need and visited sick people (Chapter 2).
Respect: Respect: The apprentice returned, said sorry and learned from his master (Chapters 6 and 7).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 7, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Tell one of the two stories to someone at home in four sentences, in your home language or in English.
